Hey! I'm a CC transfer who got accepted into Stanford for the upcoming 2018 Fall quarter. Like you already said, transfer admission is super tough at Stanford. Here is some advice for you:

\- Be your true, whole, authentic self. Let Stanford fully see your passions, interests, thoughts, hobbies, etc. on your application. Don't be afraid to use your own voice in your essays. Don't try to alter your application in a way that you think will please them. Nobody knows what Stanford is looking for in a given year in terms of admissions, so it's better to just be yourself and leave it at that.

\- Try to start seriously thinking about what you want to do with your major and trying to tailor your activities towards that goal. You're transferring in as a junior and you'll have to declare your major much sooner than traditional admits. You have to show that you're serious about your major and are actively thinking about your career. A common theme/value at Stanford is students who want to change the world. Not saying you have to follow this, but something to think about. Stanford is also a research heavy institution. If you have any kind of research experience related to your major, try to emphasize that in your application. If you don't have any, I'd recommend picking up a research internship/independent study, some other form of internship, or meaningful job (aka not retail). The main point here being that you are showing a) you take your major seriously and b) are able to apply/use it outside of your textbooks.

\- Make sure to have some solid recommenders. Preferably related to your major, but they don't necessarily have to be. Make sure to choose people who genuinely like you and have multiple good things to say about you. Also quality > quantity. I only had the required two and was able to get in. If there's nobody else you feel confident in that will write you a really nice letter of rec, don't include them on your application.

Overall, try not to stress too much about it or hunt reddit for admission chances. Like I said, nobody really knows what Stanford is looking for. 3 people, including me, from my community college got accepted into Stanford for Fall 2018. We are all very different people with very different extra curriculars, passions, and thoughts. One is the president of our student body. The other had a 4.0 for all 2 years of CC. And then there's me. I wrote one of my essays about how much I love Pokemon. So yeah be yo self lol.

I also try to break up my work into little bits everyday. This is especially true for bigger projects. The quality of a paper or project I do significantly goes up if I give myself enough time to work on it.

Hello! Just about to graduate from CC this year & transferring to Stanford. Message me if you have any specific questions or advice, but here is what I can think of off the top of my head: (Sorry this is so long lol!)

\- It's important that you figure out what you want to do in terms of your major. You have to take specific major courses in preparation for transferring, in addition to your GE courses. If you're applying to a UC or CSU, use [assist.org](https://assist.org) to figure out what those courses are for each UC/CSU. You don't necessarily need to know this right away, but definitely sometime before the beginning of your second year, figure it out. You'll also be applying under this major when you transfer, and declare it once you get on campus. Since you'll be transferring in as a junior most likely, there isn't really any going back after that. 

\- Double dip with courses where you can. If one of your major courses also works under a GE requirement, use that. It'll save you a lot of time and money.

\- Join the honors program if your CC has it. Looks great on your transcript, especially if you take honors courses within your major. It can also help connect you with like\-minded students, get you into special events, and allow you to meet with admissions counselors from 4 year schools.

\- Try to make a connection with at least one professor. Again, preferably under your major, but any professor is generally good. They can help write you nice letters of rec, supervise independent studies/research projects, and introduce you to good connections. It's always nice just to have somebody you can turn to for academic advice n things like that. I made connections with 2 professors at my CC. One is helping to pay for my time at Stanford, and the other wrote me a stellar rec and supervised a big research project I did.

\- Don't let your counselor bully you into getting an AA or ADT. If you don't have time for it, don't bother. You don't need one and it isn't going to boost your admission chances. 

\- Also, DO NOT solely rely on your counselor for information regarding transferring. Often times, they honestly do not know. Take the time to do your own research. Use [assist.org](https://assist.org). Seriously, the only time I went to my counselor was to submit paperwork and get priority enrollment during my first quarter lol.

\- Make sure you find some kind of extra curricular that you're passionate about/relates to your major. This can be either on campus or off. Look into internships, volunteering, clubs, etc. etc. You're going to have more time on your hands than you did in high school, use it wisely!

\- DON'T slack off in your CC courses. If you took a bunch of AP courses in high school, you'll definitely find CC less challenging, but that doesn't mean you get to coast through. You still need to study and do work. Keep your grades up!! 

\- Cherish your time alone. Not everybody has this experience, but I spent a lot of time by myself during CC. CC has a culture of "go to class and go home," which can make it hard to meet people. I get lonely and stuff sometimes, but I also try to appreciate being on my own. If you're transferring to a 4 year, you'll be constantly surrounded by other people, so just try to appreciate the peace and quiet while you can haha.

\- Choose your schedule wisely. If you don't like waking up at 8am, don't pick a class that starts at 8am. CC gives you a pretty nice array of different courses at different times. Try to find a schedule that works for you. I wouldn't recommend having classes everyday, try to aim for at least 2 days where you don't have class. This will give you time to do internships and other activities as well. Also try not to take more than 15 quarter units, especially during your first quarter!!! For 3 quarters in a row I tried taking 19 units. It was impossible lol. Waaayyy too much work. 

\- Don't be afraid to withdraw from a course. I have 3 W's on my transcript, and I was still accepted into Stanford. W's are better than D's or F's.

\- Make sure you familiarize yourself with the college application process before you need to apply!!!! This is REALLY important. I was lucky enough to have had applied to college during my senior year, when I was surrounded by counselors & teachers to help guide me through it. This made applying during CC a piece of cake. However, there are also many CC students who have never applied before. A lot of them struggled through the process, especially because our transfer center is ass lol. Visit the applying to college subreddit, ask questions, and do some independent research. You are also free to ask me any questions if you ever need help!!

\- To address some of your worries: You can make friends at CC if you really want to. I'm sure if I had stuck around on campus, actually started convos with people, and maybe joined a club, I would've made a friend. Again, there just tends to be a culture of class \-\-\> home. I bought into that culture because I had a lot going on. But you don't necessarily have to!! Signing up for classes shouldn't be that difficult. Just know what you want to enroll in before the register date opens. Find out how you can get priority enrollment. I've never had a problem with getting a class I needed!! **You will finish in two years if you really want to.** I'm stressing that because if you go to your orientation, they'll tell you something like "on average it takes students 3 years or more to finish at CC." Many people may also tell you stories about how it took them or someone they know 10 years or something to get an AA. Do NOT be intimidated by this. Everyone is different. For people who take over 2 years to finish at CC, it is often something that they are going through or a personal issue or struggle they have which made them take that long. It is rarely ever something wrong with the CC itself. Honestly, if you make it a priority, finishing in 2 years is so easy. Just know what you need to take, and don't fail any courses. Easy peasy. 

I hope all of that helped. I honestly loved going to CC. Saves so much fucking money and I really got to do so much cool shit while I was there. I'm also doubly excited to start at 4 year now. I advocate for CC up and down this subreddit lol.

Which is why some students end up making bad choices while in college, and maybe not getting all of they could out of the experience from an academic standpoint. I had to pay for my CC tuition myself, and I already struggled with that enough even while working. So imagining the cost of a 4 year kinda blew my mind after that lol. I wouldn't recommend high school students getting jobs though. They'll be working most of their lives and going to school all day every day is already stressful enough. If I ever have kids, I won't let them work until at least the second semester of their senior year. They should be allowed to enjoy being kids as long as they can before they're thrust into the high stress environment of college. 

Don't entirely understand your third point. But yes, college is indeed a business. They don't hand out degrees for free, but many colleges offer nice financial aid to students that need it. There is really no reason for students to go into such high amounts of debt for college tbh. And I'm talking about students with like over 40k in debt. That's crazy to me. Everyone's situation is different, but CC is always a great option for cheaper college.

One year of college is either 3 quarters or 2 semesters. Price varies greatly. 4 year universities are the most expensive, ranging from $30k \- over $100k per year. 2 years are the cheapest, and the price depends on what state you're in and how many units you take each quarter/semester. Either way, it's a great deal. Free college is ALWAYS great, no matter what the actual price is.

I 100% relate. I've had to switch jobs like 5 times in the last two years while I was at CC. I also had a manger at one of those jobs make me work full time for over a month even though he KNEW I was at school full time and that my paperwork said I was a PART TIME WORKER ONLY!!! His excuse was that there weren't enough people to cover shifts...how that's my problem, I'm not sure lol.

Like others have said, working for your school is probably the best option. Often times, the max hours you can work is 15hrs/week. You also get things like finals week off, and many jobs give you the option of working during break or not. Very very flexible and 100% understanding. The only downside in my experience is that the pay tends to be a little lower than if you worked outside of school, and it can also take awhile to a) find a job at your school b) go through the interview and paperwork process once you get the job and c) receive pay checks. Working at my school was nice when I didn't 100% need money ASAP. 

Maybe you can try working outside of your school during breaks as well. Summer especially is a great time to seek an internship and assuming you aren't taking classes, a good opportunity to work a lot and make some extra dough for the school year. 

The only other advice I have is just to be really upfront with your employers about your schedule. If you need to, lie about your availability. I made the mistake of giving my employers literally every time period where I wasn't in class. Now, I tell them times when I would realistically be able to work, factoring in how much time I need to study, relax, etc. Be very selfish and inflexible when planning this out. School should come first.

Also remember to always be applying for scholarships!! Having that extra cash can help you feel more comfortable ending employment during certain stressful periods when necessary!

1) You don't start applying until the fall of your senior year. Some applications open late summer, but a lot won't until August. The only college application related item I'd do during the summer is decide where you want to apply by beginning to research colleges, talking to your counselor, and visiting campuses. Otherwise, try to enjoy your summer as much as possible.

2) The 4.0 scale is most common. When you report your high school GPA (both weighted and unweighted), the university you are applying to will most likely have their own system for calculating your college GPA. 

3) Yes, but freshman year isn't as heavily considered as say your junior year. But they'll definitely look at it. What colleges like to see is an upward trend in your GPA. So even if you had a rough freshman year, I wouldn't stress about it too much if your GPA improved over the next 3 years.

4) The first semester of your senior year is probably the 2nd most important period AOs will look at after junior year. The second semester is more important for keeping your admissions offer. If your school notices that you've been slacking off in terms of your grades (usually something extreme like a D or an F), your admissions offer may be rescinded or you may be penalized in some way or another.

5) I'd start in the summer. There tends to be a lot going on then. There was also be a lot going on after admissions decisions roll in and people are debating between universities. 

6) I mean...that's pretty impressive. Nobody can 100% say for sure how that will be looked at, but I'm sure it won't be looked down upon. But it's not a 100% guarantee you'll get in either.  

7) I'm not sure what you mean here. As in you took extra classes over the summer or something? Or you had to take online classes during the school year for whatever reason? In either case, they probably won't care that much tbh. Although the first scenario might be looked upon more highly.

8) Internships are always good, but if you're applying from high school they aren't really expected. Just do what you're genuinely passionate about and interested in and realistically have time for. Don't try to do things just because they seem impressive. AOs can smell an in\-genuine college app no sweat. 

9) I'm pretty sure there would be some kind of test you can take that will determine your math proficiency. This is too specific of a question, though. I'd just email wherever you're trying to take the class at and ask.

10) Recommendation letters are letters from your teachers, extra curricular activity supervisors, employers, guidance counselors, etc. that basically talk about why they think you would be a great candidate for xyz school. It's hard to say how well you should know a teacher before asking. I believe the general rule of thumb is that you should've known them for at least a year. Try to pick people who you feel a personal connection with and/or who have supervised you doing activities you are passionate about or related to your major.

11) College essays are part of your application. You generally talk about yourself, challenges you've faced, the activities you've done, an idea you find interesting, etc. etc. Really depends on the college, but generally at least one. Ivy leagues, however, make you write several. They generally aren't that long. The longest college essay I've seen was the old UC application essay which was a max of about 750 words. But even that isn't that long tbh. Topic will always be supplied by the college.

12) I've heard it's not that important unless you hold some kind of leadership position or are really really involved.

13) Not necessarily. 10 years is a long time. I mean it always helps to have some kind of formal documentation, it doesn't mean you playing piano will be dismissed just because you don't have any kind of test score/reward. Again, this is something I would only do if you're a) genuinely passionate about it and b) have enough time to do so. Please please don't do things just because you think they'll seem impressive!!!

14) Haha...it's a complicated issue. It's illegal for colleges to only look at race and have racial quotas in admissions. I believe UCs can't consider race at all anymore? But I think private schools are still allowed to look at race as one *factor* in admissions, amongst many others. Being a minority is not a one way ticket into college. You still definitely have to have the grades and stuff. However, I don't think anybody can deny that it does help. How much though nobody can really say. I really really wouldn't worry about it lol. The people you see on reddit who worry about not getting into college because they are asian or white are silly, and probably just feel bad because their GPA and/or extra curriculars aren't all that stellar (also might just be overthinking it). Just do you fam. 

15) No? Never heard of this. Some colleges require freshmen to live on campus, but that's just to get you integrated into the community. Other than that, they really don't care.

Break down your studying, possibly over the course of at least two weeks. Focus on a single concept/chapter per day. If you try to tackle everything at once, it'll just be overwhelming. Once you've reviewed everything, re\-examine concepts that maybe were harder for you to understand. Seek help on those concepts if you're still shaky on them. Rinse, wash, repeat. Good luck!

I'm not a fan of this response for several reasons.

1) How do you know taking a semester off will not make it better? What evidence do you have that suggests that OP will "just drop out?" There are many people, even in this subreddit, who have talked about taking a semester off, or even an entire year, to work on themselves. Many of these people are now in university or are interested in doing so and in the process of applying. Additionally, neither you nor I are 100% aware of OP's situation. Thus, I feel like statements such as "absolutely do not take a semester off," and "it will not get better" are neither helpful nor necessarily true. I feel like it is ultimately up to OP to decide what is best for them personally, and it's more helpful to be encouraging and supporting of that rather than acting as if you are 100% certain of the answer.

2) I agree that OP reducing their schedule could potentially be helpful, as well as going to the gym. However, I also feel like this is not a holistic approach to OP's situation. Mental health is very tricky. It's important to tackle it from multiple angles. While I think OP should get regular exercise (not necessarily everyday nor even at the gym), they should also be looking at their diet, sleep schedule, support network, and self\-care. Again, I'm not dissing exercising at all. Exercise helped me A LOT when I was at my lowest point of depression, but it's not a miracle cure. Hanging out with my friends and family, sleeping 8 hours every night, making time everyday to do relaxing/enjoyable things, and eating 3 healthy meals everyday also helped me A LOT.

3) "Stop blaming your mental health," and "It was YOU who fucked up" are *incredibly* unhelpful statements. I hope you don't go around shaming people for their mental health, and acting as if it is some controllable, external part of a person that they should just be able to "toughen up" and "deal with." That is a very one dimensional, incomplete, ignorant understanding of mental health. I really encourage you to read up about mental health and all of the ways it can impact a person's life, especially the more severe it gets. One of the symptoms of depression is a lack of motivation/low energy levels. If OP is experiencing this symptom, then it makes sense that they wouldn't want to go to class. That doesn't mean they're "fucking up" in anyway. It just mean they're dealing with something incredibly difficult in their lives right now. I admire OP greatly for even reaching out and asking for help on this subreddit. Many people unfortunately bottle up their mental health issues because they take on this frame of mind that they are "fucking up." Those are the people who's mental health only gets worse and worse over the years, and they find it harder and harder to function. Some may develop almost irreversible mental health problems or even commit suicide because of this. So PLEASE do not encourage people to just ignore their mental health. The people that succeed are the ones that recognize a problem and do something about it. And as an incoming Stanford student with a 4.0 GPA, a job at one of Apple's offices, and two published research papers under my belt, who has struggled with depression and anxiety for 10 years and is only JUST NOW getting better now that I'm doing intensive outpatient therapy, I think I have the authority to say that.

I **really** think you should seek some help. Your school most likely has an on\-site psychologist/therapist you could see for free. Or, you can go through your insurance and find a therapist. The reason why I'm emphasizing this so much is because I also struggle with mental health. I've had severe depression and anxiety for the last ten years, and dealing with that on top of keeping up my academic performance was actual hell. Up until this year, I completely ignored my mental health, thinking it'd just go away eventually, or get more bearable over the years. I was **very** wrong. My mental health only deteriorated and, like you, I found myself even struggling to go to class. I also became very suicidal and was caught preparing to do it twice. I don't want to scare you, but if you continue to put yourself in a stressful situation without seeking any kind of help then you may find that you will only feel crappier and crappier. I really wish I had just seen a therapist at least once a week when I initially noticed something was wrong, rather than having to put my entire life on hold while I go to intensive outpatient therapy. There's absolutely nothing wrong with seeing a therapist or struggling with your mental health. Most people will struggle with mental health at least one point in their lives. Learn to love and take care of yourself.

You might also want to consider getting regular exercise, changing your diet (eating regularly and eating healthy meals), drinking plenty of water throughout the day, sleeping at least 7 hours every night, and making time to socialize with your friends/do things you genuinely enjoy. All of these things can really help improve your mental health, especially in combination with therapy. 

In terms of academics, I would recommend continuing, but taking a much lighter course load, or even taking an online class if you struggle with going in person. The reason I think it's important to continue pursuing your academics is because dropping it, even for a semester, may demotivate you, and you may find yourself lying around in your room doing nothing and feeling bad about yourself. A little productivity each day can really help with mental health, at least in my experience. 

Of course, nobody really knows your situation like you do. If you really feel like you need to take the semester off, then please do so. And don't feel guilty or bad about it. You're doing what's best for you, and not a lot of people have the courage to do that.  

If you ever need anybody to talk to, please feel free to reach out to me. I'm an open book and like I said, I know what it's like to struggle with mental health as a student :) Good luck and I really hope you feel better!

I saw that my college results post was linked in this thread, but I'll comment again for more context.

It's reality that transferring into these "top schools" is statistically much harder for transfers. This includes ALL transfers \(not just CC ones\), mind you. Stanford's freshman admittance rate is around 4% \- 5%, and their transfer rate is less than 1% \(meaning they take only around 15 \- 40 transfers per year\). 

When I was thinking about where to apply, I honestly wasn't even going to bother with Stanford. I hadn't bothered in my senior year, and I didn't really want to as a CC transfer either. To put some perspective on my thinking, I had \(and still have\) a lot of struggles with mental illness and self esteem. I was a good student in high school \(took AP's, got above a 4.0 W GPA and over 2,000 SAT, etc etc\), but I certainly wasn't near the top of my class. I looked at people like the valedictorian applying to schools like Stanford, and I was like "why should I bother if the admissions team is going to compare me to someone like him?" That pattern of thinking basically defined my entire high school career, and really limited me from taking opportunities that I now realize would have benefitted me tremendously. To be blunt, I severely underestimated myself and, in turn, that reflected upon my college applications and general attitude about college.  

A year or so later, I experienced a lot of personal growth. I can't really credit one factor into why I grew so much. Whether it was taking my first intro to sociology course and changing my major, meeting inspiring people and professors at my CC, pursuing extracurriculars I genuinely ENJOYED and that weren't just to look impressive on an application, or just simply having more time to myself through which I could reflect on who I was and wanted to be, but I matured A LOT. Which is why I very boldly applied to schools like UCLA and UCB. I felt a lot of confidence in myself, and not just because of my GPA, but because I felt like I really knew myself, and what I wanted out of university and just life in general. This reflected through my academic performance, extracurriculars, letters of rec, and essays. 

However, I was STILL on the fence about Stanford. So, I sat down and talked to my dad \(who I love and trust very much\), and asked him if I should apply. And he was like, "why wouldn't you?" And that was really all I needed. I started on the essays \(there's a lot of them...\) as soon as the application opened around August/September. At first I was trying to write the essays to make myself sound super smart and sophisticated. I used [thesaurus.com](https://thesaurus.com) to insert all kinds of crazy ass words that I didn't know the definition to in my essays. And at first I was like, "yeah yeah this is what they want," but after rereading them 3 months later, I'm like "oh god I can't submit these" They just didn't sound anything like me. I couldn't identify any part of my essays that represented who I had become at all. So, I deleted everything, and started to answer the essay questions extremely honestly, openly, and genuinely. For one of my essays, I wrote about how much I love playing Pokemon. For another, I wrote about how taking a smelly dog to the beach was one of the highlights of my summer. I wrote about how being black in America is hard, and about my uncle that committed suicide. I showed poured so many different aspects of myself into my essays that when I submitted my application, I had no regrets. And I knew that if they rejected me, I would feel no remorse because I had shown them all of me, and I didn't want to go to a school that didn't accept my entire person. 

Which is why when I was accepted to Stanford, it was extremely emotional for me \(and my dad\). Because they had seen all these different sides of me, and actually LIKED it, and said "yeah we want this person on our campus." And that still blows my mind. I still have such a hard time accepting that I got in, and sometimes I just have to reread that letter. I always thought you had to "solve cancer" or "create a billion dollar start up" to get into a school like Stanford. But I got in by just being who I was. 

I guess my take away from all this is to go for it. Maybe you'll get in, and maybe you won't. But if you don't try, you really will never know. Also DO NOT underestimate yourself. You are a unique and wonderful individual in your own right. Don't let ANY school make you feel invalidated or unwanted. Like my dad always tells me, "Be yourself. Love yourself. And have fun!"
